identity.title: The Polar Express: Optimal Matrix Sign Methods and their Application to the Muon Algorithm

problem.claim: Efficiently compute the polar decomposition/matrix sign function as a Muon subroutine under deep-learning priorities.

gap.claim: Classical numerical-analysis settings do not match the application’s GPU-throughput and lower-precision requirements.

contributions.claim: Introduces Polar Express, a matrix-multiplication-only polar-decomposition method whose iteration updates are chosen by minimax optimization.
Provides a worst-case error-minimization result for the update strategy, covering both early iterations and asymptotic convergence.
Addresses finite-precision use, including practical operation in bfloat16, and applies the method within Muon.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish Polar Express by adapting each iteration through a minimax optimization problem while retaining matrix-matrix multiplication updates.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report a worst-case error-minimization proof and convergence as rapidly as possible in early and asymptotic regimes.
The authors report consistent validation-loss improvements for GPT-2 trained on 1–10 billion FineWeb tokens, outperforming recent alternatives across learning rates.
The authors report that finite-precision considerations make the method practical in bfloat16.

narrative_sequence.summary: Polar decomposition and the matrix sign function are longstanding numerical-analysis problems and have become relevant to Muon.
Deep learning changes the design target toward GPU throughput rather than high precision.
Polar Express uses GPU-friendly matrix multiplications and minimax-selected updates at each iteration.
The abstract reports worst-case convergence guarantees, bfloat16 practicality, and improved GPT-2 validation loss within Muon.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns the algorithmic design—matrix multiplications and bfloat16 handling—with the deployment setting, then reports an application-level comparison in Muon.

lessons.interpretation: A strong abstract can connect method constraints, implementation choices, and downstream evidence as one application-specific argument.
lessons.application: When presenting a systems-oriented method, explicitly map each design choice to the target hardware or precision regime and report a downstream task comparison under stated conditions.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the primary contribution is purely theoretical or when downstream deployment is outside the paper’s scope.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact minimax objective, assumptions, convergence metrics, or proof conditions.
The GPT-2 comparison lacks dataset split, baseline identities, quantitative loss values, and training-control details.
The meaning of “as rapidly as possible” is not operationalized in the abstract.
